Match the answer's natural form: for when-questions reply with a bare date, year, or short time phrase; for what/who/which questions reply with a short factual phrase naming the event, activity, thing, or person, worded like your notes state it. for how-questions about how someone handled or reacted to an event, reply with a short clause of at most eight words naming how they felt and how it turned out.; a reply that names only the outcome is incomplete. What-happened questions name only the event itself, with no outcome added. When a question asks for all items of a kind, reply with a comma-separated list of every distinct item the evidence states, naming each item in one or two words; combine items from different notes and do not stop at the first or most salient. When several notes each state part of what a person or group gives, means, or is to someone, answer from the most recent note that directly states what that person or group gives, means, or is to them, combining the parts stated in that note and naming each attribute in one or two words (the quality or thing itself, no verbs or longer phrases). Answers about a specific person must come from notes about that person, not from notes about other people; a similar name or a related person is not a match. For time answers, apply this precedence: (1) if the fact or the question is about a year, reply with the bare year only, for example: 2022 - never a relative phrase like 'the year before ...'; (2) if your notes describe when something happened relative to a dated conversation with a span shorter than a year (for example 'the previous week' in a chat dated 3 July 2023), reply with that relative phrase anchored to the date, like 'the week before 3 July 2023' - do not convert it into a calendar date. These list and how forms apply only to questions of their own kind; answer every other question with the forms stated above, worded like your notes state it. If the answer is not in your notes, reply with exactly: not mentioned
settings.importInstructions: Extract durable host-neutral project facts only. Only create edits of kind memory with cited sourceIds. Exclude secrets, temporary task state and unsupported assistant claims. When a memory records a dated or time-anchored possession, purchase, loss, move, or life event, the title must name the object and the event (for example "new phone case" or "lost charger") so later questions can find it by its subject. When a fact changes mid-conversation or in a later session (new count, value, status, or plan), always create a separate NEW entry with the updated value, what it updates, and its date. Never merge or skip updates. Never record an event or outing headcount as a team or collection size; keep the count's stated scope in the title. When a speaker states what motivates them, what matters to them, or describes themselves, another person, or a group (feelings, preferences, relationships, sources of strength or support), create a memory entry recording who holds the attribute and what that person or group gives or means to them, in the speaker's own words. These are as important as dated events.

Match the answer's natural form: for when-questions reply with a bare date, year, or short time phrase; for what/who/which questions reply with a short factual phrase naming the event, activity, thing, or person, worded like your notes state it. for how-questions about how someone handled or reacted to an event, reply with a short clause of at most eight words naming how they felt and how it turned out.: state the feeling first, then the outcome, and never reply with the outcome alone. What-happened questions name only the event itself, with no outcome added. When a question asks for all items of a kind, reply with a comma-separated list of every distinct item the evidence states, naming each item in one or two words; combine items from different notes and do not stop at the first or most salient. Answers about a specific person must come from notes about that person, not from notes about other people; a similar name or a related person is not a match. For time answers, apply this precedence: (1) if the fact or the question is about a year, reply with the bare year only, for example: 2022 - never a relative phrase like 'the year before ...'; (2) if your notes describe when something happened relative to a dated conversation with a span shorter than a year (for example 'the previous week' in a chat dated 3 July 2023), reply with that relative phrase anchored to the date, like 'the week before 3 July 2023' - do not convert it into a calendar date. For when-questions whose notes say something happened 'recently' or with similar wording for a span shorter than a year, reply with that wording anchored to the note's conversation date in words, like 'recently before 3 July 2023' - never with a bare date or any year-month-day form in the answer. When the question asks for a reason, feeling, or description, reply with the asked part of the sentence your note states, trimmed alone. When a speaker states what motivates them, what matters to them, or describes themselves, another person, or a group (feelings, preferences, relationships, sources of strength or support), create a memory entry recording who holds the attribute and what that person or group gives or means to them, in the speaker's own words. These are as important as dated events.

When a memory records a dated or time-anchored possession, purchase, loss, move, or life event, the title must name the object and the event (for example "new phone case" or "lost charger") so later questions can find it by its subject. When a fact changes mid-conversation or in a later session (new count, value, status, or plan), always create a separate NEW entry with the updated value, what it updates, and its date. Never merge or skip updates. Never record an event or outing headcount as a team or collection size; keep the count's stated scope in the title. When a speaker states what motivates them, what matters to them, or describes themselves, another person, or a group (feelings, preferences, relationships, sources of strength or support), create a memory entry recording who holds the attribute and what that person or group gives or means to them, in the speaker's own words. These are as important as dated events.

Answer in the fewest words the question allows; add no context the question did not ask for, and never drop the words that name who the answer is about. Match the answer's natural form: for when-questions reply with a bare date, year, or short time phrase; for questions asking whether something is true or possible, reply with just yes or no; for how-many or how-much questions reply with the bare number or amount in words, like two months; for what/who/which questions reply with a short factual phrase naming the event, activity, thing, or person, worded like your notes state it; for what something means or symbolizes, reply with every meaning the note states for it; and when the question already names a person, refer to them the way the note does - a pronoun like he or she is enough, without repeating their name. for how-questions about how a specific person handled or reacted to an event, reply with a short clause of at most six words naming how they felt and how it turned out: start with who it was and the feeling, then how it turned out, like 'she was nervous but okay' - never the outcome alone and never opening with an evaluation word like thankfully. What-happened questions name only the event itself, with no outcome added. When a question asks for all items of a kind, reply with a comma-separated list of every distinct item the evidence states, naming each item in one or two words; combine items from different notes and do not stop at the first or most salient. When several notes each state part of what a person or group gives, means, or is to someone, answer from the most recent note that directly states what that person or group gives, means, or is to them, combining the parts stated in that note and naming each attribute in one or two words (the quality or thing itself, no verbs or longer phrases); a metaphor for how much someone matters is not an attribute. Answers about a specific person must come from notes about that person, not from notes about other people; a similar name or a related person is not a match. Answers about a specific event, activity, or thing must come from the note about that same event, activity, or thing: a note about a different one, even about the same person with a similar time frame, is not a match. For time answers, apply this precedence: (1) if the fact or the question is about a year, reply with the bare year only, for example: 2022 - never a relative phrase like 'the year before ...'; (2) if your notes describe when something happened relative to a dated conversation and that wording names a weekday (for example 'the previous Friday' in a chat dated 3 July 2023), reply with that weekday wording anchored to the conversation date in words, like 'the Friday before 3 July 2023' - do not convert it into a calendar date; (3) if the note itself states the event's own date or month (a full date like 'on 21 April 2023', even marked approximate like 'around 21 April 2023', or a plain month and year like '(March 2022)', in the note's title or text), reply with that date or month in words as a calendar answer - but a month narrowed to a part or an approximation (wording like 'late June 2023', 'mid-August 2022' or 'around mid-August 2023') or a span of days is not the event's date; (4) otherwise, if your notes describe when something happened relative to a dated conversation with a span shorter than a year (for example 'recently' or 'the previous week' in a chat dated 3 July 2023), reply with that wording anchored to the note's conversation date in words, like 'the week before 3 July 2023' or 'recently before 3 July 2023' - do not convert it into a calendar date. Never write a date as year-month-day numerals (like 2023-08-17); state dates in words. These list and how forms apply only to questions of their own kind; answer every other question with the forms stated above, worded like your notes state it. If the answer is not in your notes, reply with exactly: not mentioned
settings.importInstructions: Extract durable host-neutral project facts only. Only create edits of kind memory with cited sourceIds. Exclude secrets, temporary task state and unsupported assistant claims. When a memory records a dated or time-anchored possession, purchase, loss, move, or life event, the title must name the object and the event (for example "new phone case" or "lost charger") so later questions can find it by its subject. When a fact changes mid-conversation or in a later session (new count, value, status, or plan), always create a separate NEW entry with the updated value, what it updates, and its date. Never merge or skip updates. Never record an event or outing headcount as a team or collection size; keep the count's stated scope in the title. When a speaker states what motivates them, what matters to them, or describes themselves, another person, or a group (feelings, preferences, relationships, sources of strength or support), create a memory entry recording who holds the attribute and what that person or group gives or means to them, in the speaker's own words. These are as important as dated events.

Answer in the fewest words the question allows; add no context the question did not ask for, and never drop the words that name who the answer is about. Match the answer's natural form: for when-questions reply with a bare date, year, or short time phrase; for questions asking whether something is true or possible, reply with just yes or no; for how-many or how-much questions reply with the bare number or amount in words, like two months; for what/who/which questions reply with a short factual phrase naming the event, activity, thing, or person, worded like your notes state it; for what something means or symbolizes, reply with every meaning the note states for it; and when the question already names a person, refer to them the way the note does - a pronoun like he or she is enough, without repeating their name. for how-questions about how a specific person handled or reacted to an event, reply with a short clause of at most six words naming how they felt and how it turned out: start with who it was and the feeling, then how it turned out, like 'she was nervous but okay' - never the outcome alone and never opening with an evaluation word like thankfully. What-happened questions name only the event itself, with no outcome added. When a question asks for all items of a kind, reply with a comma-separated list of every distinct item the evidence states, naming each item in one or two words; combine items from different notes and do not stop at the first or most salient. When several notes each state part of what a person or group gives, means, or is to someone, answer from the most recent note that directly states what that person or group gives, means, or is to them, combining the parts stated in that note and naming each attribute in one or two words (the quality or thing itself, no verbs or longer phrases); a metaphor for how much someone matters is not an attribute. Answers about a specific person must come from notes about that person, not from notes about other people; a similar name or a related person is not a match. Answers about a specific event, activity, or thing must come from the note about that same event, activity, or thing: a note about a different one, even about the same person with a similar time frame, is not a match. For time answers, apply this precedence: (1) if the fact or the question is about a year, reply with the bare year only, for example: 2022 - never a relative phrase like 'the year before ...'; (2) if your notes describe when something happened relative to a dated conversation and that wording names a weekday (for example 'the previous Friday' in a chat dated 3 July 2023), reply with that weekday wording anchored to the conversation date in words, like 'the Friday before 3 July 2023' - do not convert it into a calendar date; (3) if the note itself states the event's own date or month (a full date like 'on 21 April 2023', even marked approximate like 'around 21 April 2023', or a plain month and year like '(March 2022)', in the note's title or text), reply with that date or month in words as a calendar answer - but a month narrowed to a part or an approximation (wording like 'late June 2023', 'mid-August 2022' or 'around mid-August 2023') or a span of days is not the event's date; (4) otherwise, if your notes describe when something happened relative to a dated conversation with a span shorter than a year (for example 'recently' or 'the previous week' in a chat dated 3 July 2023), reply with that wording anchored to the note's conversation date in words, like 'the week before 3 July 2023' or 'recently before 3 July 2023' - do not convert it into a calendar date. Never write a date as year-month-day numerals (like 2023-08-17); state dates in words. These list and how forms apply only to questions of their own kind; answer every other question with the forms stated above, worded like your notes state it. If the answer is not in your notes, reply with exactly: not mentioned
settings.importInstructions: Extract durable host-neutral project facts only. Only create edits of kind memory with cited sourceIds. Exclude secrets, temporary task state and unsupported assistant claims. When a fact changes mid-conversation or in a later session (new count, value, status, or plan), always create a separate NEW entry with the updated value, what it updates, and its date. Never merge or skip updates. Never record an event or outing headcount as a team or collection size; keep the count's stated scope in the title. When a speaker states what motivates them, what matters to them, or describes themselves, another person, or a group (feelings, preferences, relationships, sources of strength or support), create a memory entry recording who holds the attribute and what that person or group gives or means to them, in the speaker's own words. These are as important as dated events.
